utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you quality case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused and everyone else in the courtroom. As you're well aware, I'll be giving the floor to the parties to comment on the reduction of time allocated for the presentation of the Prosecution case, but I would like to congratulate Mr. Karnavas for having been elected as president of the Defence counsel. I do this on behalf of all the Judges, and I'm sure that his competence will be of great benefit for all of us and to the Rules Committee as well. On behalf of the Judges, I'd like to congratulate Mr. Karnavas. As I said, I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution for 15 minutes so that they can make known their position as far as the plan to reduce the time granted to them for their case is concerned. Mr. Scott, you have the floor for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon. As the Prosecution was thinking about these -- this question, we were -- reflected back on a similar presentation that we made to the Chamber before the trial started and it seems to us that some of those points are equally relevant today and I'll try to move as quickly as possible but at the same time address points that are extremely important, obviously to the Prosecution, and I think to everyone in the courtroom. And I have taken a liberty of putting a few points on the PowerPoint presentation so I would ask our case manager to pull up the first slide. Mr. President and Your Honours, I start with this slide just to remind everyone that the entire Tribunal, not just the Office of the Prosecutor, moved in the direction of these larger so-called megatrials as a move to greater overall efficiency in completing the docket, the heavy docket of this institution. Nonetheless, it had to be known that these megatrials, these leadership trials would be large, difficult and complex and certainly in conducting these trials it should not be done to the disadvantage or the prejudice of the Prosecution. I also start, of course, with the fundamental notion that the Prosecution and in its representation of the victims of the alleged crimes and the international community is fully entitled to a fair trial, a fair trial just as equal -- equally fair to the Prosecution as to the Defence. Not almost as fair, not somewhat as fair, just equally as fair the -- as to the Defence, no more and no less. We start with that as our fundamental premise. Indeed, this institution has recognised the importance and the burden the Prosecution has in telling an entire story and putting on its case. Unlike the Defence, of course, we have the burden to present our entire affirmative case. In the absence of agreement we simply have no alternative but to put on the evidence that we believe is reasonably necessary to sustain the burden that we shoulder. Based on these premises, Your Honours, the Prosecution starts -- in fact, starts from the premise that, and certainly the hope that the Chamber intends to give and will give the Prosecution and the victims and the international community a fair trial. Based on this, we have to assume or understand that the Chamber has some ideas in mind on how to move the trial more efficiently but at the same time fairly, in fairness to both the Defence and in fairness to the Prosecution, and to the victims and to the international community. Because of this, Your Honours, the Prosecution cannot really fully state its position today without knowing additionally what steps the Chamber has in mind for conducting the trial more efficiently, because certainly, and it is our bottom line position, certainly it would not be fair, it is not fair, to simply make a dramatic cut in the Prosecution's case with a full burden and the consequences of efficiency only being shouldered by the Prosecution to it's prejudice. It is unfair and really not meaningful ultimately, Your Honours, to talk about measuring the pace of the trial according to a 12-month calendar, because a calendar can mean anything. It depends on how it's defined. A calendar year can mean anything from 52 five-day weeks, eight hours a day. It can mean 30 weeks a year, two days a week. It simply means nothing until defined. In this trial, a Prlic trial year is approximately 40 weeks -- taking into account all the holidays and recesses, 40 weeks, four days a week - approximately, and not counting the breaks - in actual courtroom time, approximately four hours. That equals a trial year of 640 hours. Now, of course in this context, Your Honours, the Prosecution, just as the Defence, can only be accountable for its own time. We have no control over the -- what the Defence does or what the Chamber does. Questions that the Judges ask, the procedural matters, we have no way of controlling that and, certainly, Your Honour, we cannot be held responsible or accountable for anything but our own time. To date the Prosecution has been averaging approximately five and a half hours a week of direct examination time. Now, the basic numbers that we're looking at then, as of the numbers that the registry, and thanks to the registry, produced on Friday, as of the 2nd of November we have -- the trial has take approximately 330 hours and 30 minutes. The Defence cross-examinations have taken approximately 126 hours, procedural matters and Judges' questions have taken almost 105 hours, and the Prosecution's time has taken a little less than 103 hours. I note, Your Honours, that of the three categories the Prosecution is at the bottom of the list. The bottom of the list. The basic numbers, then. We have called 44 Prosecution witnesses in 75 days. Of course, we've also tendered two 92 bis witnesses so far that have been accepted, so we've actually presented 46 witnesses to the Chamber so far. Again, a trial day is four hours. A trial week is 16 hours. The Prosecution has used a total of 102 hours and 40 minutes. Now, you can do the math and that's -- for 44 witnesses, that's an average of 2.3 hours per witness. Of course some have been longer, the experts, some of the political witnesses, some might call policy witnesses; some have been shorter. And many of the crime base witnesses will be shorter. But, Your Honours, I must say I have been doing this work now for 26, 27 years and I've conducted a lot of large, complex cases and there is no -- with all respect there is no intellectually honest, fair-minded person who can say an average of 2.3 hours to conduct an examination - on average - of witnesses is unreasonable and dilatory. It is moving with remarkable speed given a case of this size and complexity. At the beginning, the Prosecution and the Chamber asked this question before trial, computed that we would need based on our assessment approximately 450 hours of direct examination. That's what we told the Chamber in April. We remind the Chamber that the Chamber's already cut 50 hours from our case before what it is considering now. To cut an additional 100 hours would mean cutting a full third of the Prosecution's original time estimate which we believe was realistic based on an actual analysis of our case. Now, can steps be taken to work more efficiently? The Prosecution, and I'm sure the Defence will say the same, the Prosecution will certainly work with the Chamber to find ways to make the trial proceedings more efficient, if this can be accomplished in a fair way and without the full burden of any efficiencies being visited only on the Prosecution, which in our respect -- in our respectful submission, Your Honours, would be completely unfair. Not only unfair to the Prosecution, this Prosecution team, but unfair to the victims who deserve a full day in court and they deserve to have their claims heard and fairly adjudicated, and the international community deserves a fair trial. We have tried -- we've been -- various efforts to identify and possibly narrow the disputed facts. We spent a huge amount of effort in the pre-trial phrase to do that through exchanges of proposed agreed facts. We have continued doing that. The next slide. Even in the past few weeks. We have submitted additional proposals to the Defence since the end of August for possible agreement as to certain -- the basic facts and certain facts in the Prozor crime base area, the Gornji Vakuf crime base, and now we're starting today the Jablanica crime base. Unfortunately this has not been productive. Again, Your Honour, that means that the Prosecution has no alternative but to present its full case, all of its evidence on each element of each offence in a way that we believe satisfies the burden of proof that we have. We said at the beginning of trial that we intended to make extensive use of Rule 92 bis, and we hoped many of these witnesses, especially as to crime base, especially as to witnesses who have testified before, would not have to come for additional cross-examination. I just -- I remind the Chamber that there are two -- at least two motions pending now for two witnesses to be accepted on a 92 bis basis without cross-examination. We have talked about the use of written evidence. This institution has certainly by the rules committee and by the Plenary Sessions indicated a desire and a decision to go in the direction of more written evidence, not the strong preference for oral evidence that existed at the beginning of this institution some years ago, but to accept more evidence in writing. We have stated our intention to use those tools to the full advantage and we've attempted and will continue to attempt to do so. We've also had a number of discussions about how exhibits might be taken and handled more efficiently, and Chamber just last week invited us to make submissions today, other submissions today, on how that might be done, and we continue to urge the Chamber, as you will see in our submissions today, to adopt a flexible approach to the reception and the admission of documentary evidence that is fully consistent with the jurisprudence and practice of this institution. Can the day-to-day mode of conducting trial be revised to work more efficiently? Maybe the Prosecution has ideas. Maybe the Prosecution has some ideas. Maybe the Chamber has ideas. Perhaps the day-to-day questioning of the witnesses can be taken in a more efficient manner. I simply put that out for additional discussion. The Defence cases. I say this, Your Honour, not to cast any stones but of course the Prosecution must take the position that if such stringent time limits are put on the Prosecution case we can only insist, we will only be able to insist that very same stringent positions be put on the Defence cases. If the Prosecution case is limited to 300 hours we would understand the Chamber to be saying the six Defence cases in total would be limited to 300 hours, and I can assure the Court that we would be very unhappy if we found that the same type time constraints imposed on the Prosecution were not placed on the Defence. Finally, as we said again in our submissions in April, if the Chamber essentially puts us in a position with all respect of proving what we might consider an extremely limited, rather skeletal case, then we would expect and we would ask and we would hope that the Chamber will then give us the opportunity to put on a substantial rebuttal case once additional issues are identified in the course of the Defence cases, because we will not under any circumstance, unless something dramatically different is doing -- is done - excuse me - other than simply whack off a hundred hours of the Prosecution case, we will not be able to put on a fair and reasonable case. That is our submission, Your Honour. We -- as I said, we stand ready to work with the Chamber on all levels to find more efficient ways to proceed in a way that that burden is shared by all in the courtroom, including the Defence and, with the greatest of respect, including the Chamber and its staff and the Prosecution, and without prejudice to the Prosecution and the victims and the international community. I must say, Your Honour, I must conclude my remarks by saying the victims of this case in particular, the victims of the alleged crimes, deserve a fair trial. Anything less than that, anything less than that would be a shame. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your very interesting comments, Mr. Scott, and in particular the slides that we saw were very useful. It was possible for us to follow what you were saying more clearly as a result of the use of the slides. So thank you for this very efficient statement of your position which will make it easier for the Judges to discuss the matter later on. But we will now be paying just as much attention to what the Defence has to say. The Defence has, roughly speaking, the same amount of time at their disposal. I believe Mr. Murphy will be taking the floor on behalf of the Defence teams. Mr. Murphy, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. There are two issues that will Trial Chamber has asked us to address today. One relates specifically to the possible modification of the decision on evidence of the 13th of July, and then there's the more general question of the limitation of time that Mr. Scott has just dealt with, and perhaps it would be convenient if I were to begin with a shorter subject, which is the decision of the 13th of July. As I understand it, Your Honour, we -- the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the decision of the 13th of July should essentially remain in effect but with some modification to provide some flexibility for statements that cannot be shown to witnesses in the course of direct examination. Your Honour, the Defence had some discussion on this, and we do have a proposal to make which I will make now, and there will be time for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to reflect on it. We suggest that one method of dealing with this would be to have a witness execute an additional witness statement limited to the question of the identification of documents with which that witness is familiar, and that would be a statement independent of any other evidence that the witness might give, and it could be disclosed to the Defence at some reasonable time beforehand, and that -- that statement, Your Honour, could then be tendered under Rule 89(F). We would only ask in that event that the Defence be given a reasonable amount of time for cross-examination. It may be that in some cases the witness would have nothing else to give evidence about except to identify certain documents. It may be that, on the other hand, this evidence would be additional to other matters the witness deals with. But it would be a relatively simple matter for the Trial Chamber to provide the Defence with a little additional time, with the understanding that that would be dedicated exclusively to any necessary cross-examination about the documents in question. Your Honour, we have two other smaller proposals that might assist. The -- the Trial Chamber has referred to difficulties in complying with guideline 6 of the order of the 13th of July in explaining to the Trial Chamber why a particular document is necessary for the case. I only have the French version of the order with me today, but the wording, Your Honour, in that version: "Raisons pour lesquelles la partie estime que cette piece est indispensable a la determination de l'affaire." Your Honour, we would submit that that provision may be unnecessary. We would recommend that it simply be deleted. If a party -- if a party can demonstrate that the document is in fact relevant and has some probative value, we submit that that would be a sufficient premise for the motion, and it would also remove any suggestion that if the Trial Chamber finds a document to be necessary or "indispensable", it would avoid any suggestion that the Trial Chamber simply by admitting it is assigning necessarily degree of weight to that particular document that the word "indispensable" rather suggests. So we would suggest that that might make the guidelines somewhat easier to work with. The last thing, Your Honour, is in the very first line of guideline 6. There is a reference to the Prosecution as being the party which is entitled to make a motion. We would anticipate, Your Honour, that the Defence might eventually be in the same position and we would invite the Trial Chamber to consider amending the first line to read "The parties," rather than simply "the Prosecution" would be entitled to make such a motion. Your Honour, the second matter I have to deal with is the broader question of the further limitation of time that Mr. Scott has just dealt with, and by way of introduction to that, I would like to say, Your Honours, that like Mr. Scott I have been engaged in legal practice for many years, more than 35 years, and it's a tradition in my jurisdiction that with some degree of seniority counsel has some entitlement to address a Trial Court with a little more candor than might be the case with a more junior member of the bar, while of course being respectful. And I hope Your Honours know by now that I have the utmost respect for each member of the Trial Chamber. Your Honour, the first thing I want to say is that the Defence supports the Prosecution's position as expressed by Mr. Scott today. This is a case of enormous size and complexity. Now, we on the Defence side have in the past advocated that the indictment should be reduced in size, and it has been our consistent position that if that had been done, the trial would be much smaller in scope and would last for a shorter period of time. But given that that has not happened, we take the position that the Prosecution is entitled to a fair trial and to present its case in as much fullness as it considers necessary. We say that, Your Honour, both as a matter of principle and -- and, to be quite candid, as a matter of self-interest, because as Mr. Scott has indicated today quite logically, what has happened to the Prosecution could equally well some months from now be happening to the Defence, and we would be opposed to that. And candidly, Your Honour, in 35 years of legal practice, I have never known a Trial Chamber to step in and cut a party's time to such a drastic degree, especially when the trial has been under way for something like six months. Your Honour, it seems to the Defence that the focus of this trial has somewhat shifted from being a search for truth in this very complex case to being an exercise to complete it within deadlines that have been imposed from outside. A good example of that which affects the Defence as well as the Prosecution is the indication given by the Trial Chamber that you intend to deduct time for objections from the time of the party who makes those objections. Leaving aside the practical problems, for example, that certain counsel tend to make objections on behalf of all the accused, it puts us in a conflict in representing our clients between exercising two very important functions, both of which are elements of a fair trial. One is engaging in a full cross-examination, and one is making a record through objections. And, as Your Honours know, the Appeals Chamber has repeatedly taken the position that if one does not make a record at trial then the Appeals Chamber will not consider that ground of appeal, if necessary, later on in the proceedings. So we're in the position now where we must trade time exercising one important function for time exercising another, but it's our submission that the accused is fully entitled to a fair trial and that involves counsel having the full latitude to exercise both of those important functions. There's also, Your Honour, an issue of due process. Because we're now in the position where this Trial Chamber has imposed restrictions of time on every aspect of the trial, whereas accused who are currently in other trials are not subject to those restrictions, and indeed those restrictions have not been applied to previous trials in this Tribunal, and I take as an example the trial of General Blaskic, which obviously is connected closely with this case, where there was one accused, and allowing for the fact that there was a certain period when the trial would meet and then recess quite frequently, that trial took approximately two years to conduct. Now, Your Honours, it seems to us looking over all the changes that have been made that what has happened here is not simply a change in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, but what has happened here is something of a change in the mode of trial itself. In 1994, Judge Cassese, the first President of the Tribunal, on the occasion of adopting the Rules of Procedure and Evidence made a statement in which he said the mode of trial of the Tribunal was intended to be adversarial, but very recently Judge Pocar, in his address to the United Nations, said that the adversarial mode of trial had to some extent now been superseded by a system of trial in which there was a much greater degree of judicial control. Your Honour, the Defence has no objection to the inquisitorial mode of trial as such. We recognise that it can be perfectly fair. But the problem is that there is certain procedural protections that have to be in place under that system, including having a Prosecutor who has the obligation to investigate in the interests of all parties and to produce a dossier of the evidence. And in addition, the change of mode of trial has been introduced several months into the trial itself. Now, Your Honour, we -- we on the Defence side recognise that the Judges of the Trial Chamber are very concerned with the issue of fairness, and I hope that that will not be in doubt by virtue of anything that I'm saying, but the Defence takes the position that this change of the mode of trial and particularly with the restriction on time has made the trial unfair both from the point of view of the Prosecution and the Defence. And finally, Your Honour, I draw attention to this: That there can be no fair trial without a fully independent judiciary. And from the moment when the conduct of the trial is governed by the completion strategy rather than the considerations of fairness to the parties, the independence of the judiciary is clearly compromised. And because we know that that is not Your Honours' intention, we wish to draw your attention respectfully at this time so that it can be considered before the trial proceeds any further. Because, Your Honour, what's at stake, as Mr. Scott so eloquently indicated, is also the fairness of the trial to the international community and, in part, the legacy of this Tribunal itself. Your Honour, I -- I want to conclude, if Your Honours will allow me, by saying one other thing very briefly. Like all Defence lawyers, from time to time I make objections and file motions when I think something has gone wrong with the trial, but like many other lawyers, I'm often invited to speak at forums outside the -- the premises, and on those occasions invariably defend the fairness of this Tribunal and its procedures, and I become angry if somebody criticises my Tribunal on those occasions. And, Your Honour, the Defence, just as much as the Prosecution, is invested in the success of this trial, obviously for different reasons, and we will work with the Trial Chamber to make sure that we work to the maximum degree of efficiency, and we invite the Trial Chamber to -- to reprimand us whenever we do not. But, Your Honour, what -- what we cannot, with all due respect, agree to is having the -- the trial compromised by deference to external deadlines. Your Honour, this has been, candidly, one of the most difficult submissions I have made in 35 years of legal practice. I'm glad that it's over, and I hope that the Trial Chamber will to some extent be assisted by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy. We listened with attention to what you've said, and of course we're going to examine the points one by one, everything that you put forward, and we will particularly bear in mind everything that you said. Now, you raised a subject which should be discussed today, that is to say the admissibility of exhibits, and I'll briefly give the floor to the Prosecution for them to tell me their point of view, because this was not mentioned when Mr. Scott was speaking a moment ago. To summarise, you have made a proposal, an innovative one, and extremely interesting at that, which is if a witness has the possibility of writing out a written statement about documents as well, so that the Prosecution need not present the documents to him during the examination-in-chief and which would later on allow the Defence to cross-examine on those exhibits. So that's an interesting proposal and it would be based on 89(F), Rule 89(F). You have also proposed two technical invasions, one with respect to paragraph 6 of our decision, of our ruling which related to the order "indispensable." It is the view of the Chamber that certain documents could be admitted if, in the eyes of the party presenting the document are truly indispensable, that is to say that they have a probative value and pertinence and relevance to a maximum level, and others documents that are not at that character would not be admitted. And also the third point, a technical one, and you're quite right there, we substitute the term "Prosecution" for "parties." But you did not respond to the question of substance, which is that we envisaged the admission of documents without any witness at all. You did not address that matter and made no proposals. Mr. Scott, would you like to respond in written form or orally to that first part of Mr. Murphy's intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Excuse me. We had understood and perhaps wrongly, but we had understood that this would be a written submission and we have filed or are in the process of filing a written submission on this point today. I do appreciate what Mr. Murphy has said, and we would like to consider and take that further on board. I think the Chamber -- I think the Chamber has pointed out -- made the point that we would most make, and I guess our principal concern has been, and speaking again with full candour, not the documents that cannot be put in through a witness for various reasons, again because of time constraints or because of witness unavailability or what have you. Our basic proposal, Your Honour, in a nutshell is that virtually, we believe, respectfully, that virtually every trial that's been conducted in this institution, there has to be a reasonable mechanism for tendering at least a certain amount of evidence, some say from counsel table or from the bar table. We believe that's fully consistent with the Tribunal jurisprudence and practice, and in our submission we outline that in more detail. I am encouraged and I would take the opportunity to say that what Mr. Murphy says, I think about relevance, we would agree. I think the primary factor here is, is a document relevant? Is it something that will assist the Chamber in conducting ultimately its task of adjudicating this case? Clearly all the jurisprudence, all the jurisprudence is that this Tribunal is not built on technical rules of evidence. It is to receive evidence in an inclusion -- if you will, an inclusionary rather than an exclusionary way. And in that context, it is indeed the relevance of the document of the material that is the key criteria. We think that criteria can be satisfied in a way, again, by tendering exhibits through -- from counsel table, and the counsel, whether it's the Defence or the Prosecution, we would certainly agree with Mr. Murphy that if it's -- if the Prosecution can do it then certainly the Defence has to be able to do it as well, that if the parties can put forward material that is relevant, can be explained as relevant, that that is the principal criterion. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to read your written submission, since you have indicated to us that that is what you're going to do and that you filed them this morning. I didn't know about that. And in light of what Mr. Murphy has told us in his proposals as well as all the written submissions, we will take everything into account and give a ruling. I saw Mr. Praljak on his feet. Mr. Praljak, just briefly, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, I will be brief, Your Honour. I'll speak in my own name but I think the accused agree. We would like to see the victims receive satisfaction. We would like -- we are in detention, that is to say, we are not at liberty, and we continue to be in detention. We, too, would like to have the truth prevail at this Tribunal and come out. But I would like to express my concern once again on concepts. When we say "government," when we say "army," when we use those concepts and terms, "political situation," being an another, the influence of the international community, Yugoslavia, embargo, all those terms and concepts in order to arrive at our basic goal here, which is to determine what could have been done and what a person given a situation and circumstance could have done. We saw with regret people here who were crime base witnesses, who were raped or persons being killed, et cetera, but 90 per cent of them -- from 90 per cent of them we did not learn who killed these people, that proceedings had not been taken. That is having we heard about. We heard about these people, perpetrators going free and walking B but we didn't actually hear who those people were. Now, a society in war and a society out of war is a very complicated thing with thousands of phenomena making up its individual parts. So without being able to compare concepts such as armies, the American army in Iraq and situations which get out of hand and the possibility of controlling the unrest in France just because somebody in a certain street in a certain town assumed a certain position, still does not mean that there is enough power and authority to prevent these things from happening. Now, because we use concepts in this trial such as the army and the fact that the German government, the German army, the German people learned, for example, that in 2002 German soldiers had photographs taken with the heads decapitated heads of individuals, skulls, and so on. Or in Abu Ghraib just because a photographer uncovered this to the press in other areas, in England, for example, did this fact come out. So I think we're moving towards a situation where we are going to look at the subject of crime and punishment and who is to blame just because we do not have God. Now, you asked us to look at the different concepts of a state and army, a well-ordered state, a well-ordered army or governments which -- governments in form with no ministers, ministers who have no telephones, that we should clarify comparative models. I don't know. Perhaps New Orleans after the flood. Look at situations like that. But it is not the head of -- the chief of police or mayor that is held responsible. I don't say that there is no other way of doing this, but we still don't have this linkage, this mechanism for linking up all these different things, and I think that this will lead us to ascribe blame on people who could have not -- not have done otherwise. Now, our lives have been disrupted, at least mine has over the past six or seven years, because when journalists write about me they always say that I'm a war criminal. They never say "alleged war criminal" or that I have been accused of such, and my life is not worth a penny unless I can establish here in the trial where the limits of my blame go, how far I am responsible, how far I am not responsible given the political climate and other circumstances and so on and so forth. So that's what I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. We listened to what you said. We have heard you, and we shall have that as food for thought, and we shall of course be making a ruling. I can see that Mr. Prlic would like to rise. I'll give him a few moments to say what he wants to say. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to say that certain concepts ought to be cleared up. I don't know what the word means for "deadlines" and time restrictions. In respect of what? To -- we started -- we went to trial two years after the indictment had been raised, and now the trial will last three years. If we continue working at this tempo, which we do not conduct enough time to conduct cross-examination of key witnesses that won't come back to this Tribunal, that means another five years, which makes it a total of seven years, the timeframe of seven years. And nothing can be considered to be big or small unless it is compared to something else. And certain measures seem at first glance to promote matters whereas they don't really. 92 ter prolongs the trial and not speeds it up, because we see that we're given 20 minutes now for witnesses that had previously been allotted two hours. That's my first point. Secondly, when I speak of overall time and total time, it is not up to us. It is not our responsibility. We have come to confront the indictments that have been raised against us. We have briefs written to the form of the indictment, objections to the form of the indictment. They were refused. We asked for repeated confirmation, confirmation de novo, with respect to the new circumstances. That was refused too. We called for a separation of trial and that was refused too. I don't accept the word "Defence," Defence teams. There are various Defence teams here, six in fact. You said that there are 1.800 acts here with 14 degrees of responsibility. If we divide that up with the total amount of time given to one Defence team, 66 hours, compared to the initial 400, then it would appear that for each act and specific form of responsibility and accountability the Defence has a little over seven seconds for cross-examination. If we add to this when the Defence puts forward its case, then this is 15 seconds for each act and form of responsibility and accountability that is specified in the indictment, the counts in the indictment. Now, what I do want to say when I have said all this? You're going to find a situation which even Kafka envisaged. We have to give up our rights for a speedy trial and ask you to leave us in prison for another two years, if the trial were to be a fair and just trial. So please understand our position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Prlic, for those calculations and you are quite true that there are 1.800 crimes, and if you divide -- your time by the number of crimes that will give you just a few seconds per crime, per act, criminal act. That is something that we're going to bear in mind in our deliberations. So let me say that everything the parties have just said will be analysed, dissected, and integrated into our ultimate ruling in response to the questions raised and the elements put forward by both parties. Or all three parties. I see the President of the Defence Counsel Council on his feet, so if Mr. Karnavas would like to stand and say something of particular interest he can go ahead. If not, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to point out to the Trial Chamber that what Mr. Prlic said and others have said including, you know, Mr. Praljak, that effectively they have -- they have and are willing to waive what has been commented here as this right to an expeditious trial or an expedient trial. Some would say, and I'm one of them, that the right to an expeditious trial is for the pre-trial phase with the understanding that the trial phase is held within a reasonable period of time. That's not happening in this Tribunal. Most people at the pre-trial stage will wait three, four, five years before they get to trial. But if such a right exists and is interpreted, as I believe some would interpret it, that is that the trial process is expeditious. There is an unequivocal waiver on the record of this particular right with the understanding of rather having an expedient trial or fast trial they would like to have a trial within a reasonable amount of time allowing the accused, each accused, to put on their case, recognising that it's perhaps insufficient for the Trial Chamber to tell the Defence, "Well, you can bring that up on your case." Because that assumes that we have a case to answer, and it does effectively shift the burden onto the Defence. I think we have been moving in a rather fast pace, and I just want to make sure that we don't move so fast that at the end we're all blamed and -- with the outcome. And when I say "all," both parties and -- as well as the Bench. But the record has been made, Your Honours, that they're willing -- each accused is essentially willing to waive this right with the understanding that the trial be held within a reasonable period of time. And that waiver -- or that right incidentally can be waived. It's not such a -- like a right of a fair trial. You can't waive that. You're shaking your head, Judge Trechsel, but you can waive your right to assist in your own defence. You can waive your right against self-incrimination and testify. You can waive your right -- there are some rights that are waivable to a certain extent. Obviously, and that's -- that's my whole point, that they're waiving it to the extent that they're saying, "Give us a trial within a reasonable period of time," and that's -- that's what I meant. So I hope that clears any misunderstandings regarding that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to give floor to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to make clear that apparently my non-verbal language can lead to misunderstandings. I have not shaken my head, which would be turning it like this, but I have waved it, which indicates deeper thought, which perhaps you do not think I'm able of, but maybe I'm not, but I try to. I would like to add one or two points. First, indeed I am not quite sure to which extent one party, namely the Defence, can, as it were, unilaterally waive the right to an expeditious trial. Here the Prosecution goes in the same sense but it is a question I think which is not really settled in any -- clearly settled in any case law. That was my -- my doubts. I am impressed, and Mr. Murphy has referred to it more or less in passing, that there is one element which we all are aware of. So far there is a clear opinion of the counts of the Security Council of the United Nations that trials in first instance must be terminated by the end of 2008, and one permanent member, Russia, "pour lesquelles la partie", indicates very clearly that they will veto any prolongation of the existence of this trial, and I would have hoped that those present would address with some substance this situation which I'm afraid is beyond the control of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Not everyone at the same time, perhaps. Mr. Karnavas first and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could go just very quickly, and I mentioned this before. What in essence is occurring or has occurred, the Security Council has placed the Tribunal and the Judges in particular in a rather untenable position, because they have to decide whether they're going to serve the interests of the Security Council which created this -- this institution, which funds it, which drafted or approved the Statute, or will they be serving the interests of justice. And I would say that for me it is a very easy answer. Judges can only serve the interests of justice and that's it. The Security Council, if they want to close down the institution in the middle of a trial, let them do so. Shame on them. They established it; they have to fund it. I think Judge Hunt was rather precise and rather eloquent when he said, "If the international community wishes to have tribunals of this nature then they need to fund them." And they can't simply shift the burden onto the Judges to do the Security Council's dirty work, as it were, to say, "You figure out a way of finishing a trial within this period of time because there is no more funding," and then have you share the responsibility, share the burden, ensure -- and effectively take on the shame that will follow if later on it turns out that the accused or the Prosecution, the victims, did not have a fair -- a fair trial, did not have a fair day in this courtroom. And I think that is something that unfortunately no one wishes to discuss but that is what is happening. We like to think about this, having an expeditious trial, I hear this so often these days, and for me it's kind of a buzzword. I must say and I must speak very openly and honestly. To me that's completion strategy talk. Years ago we didn't talk about completion strategy, and nobody dared talk about it last year or the year before. Now we're talking about it openly and candidly. But I think that the Judges have to stand firm and say, "We cannot provide a trial within this amount of time given the complexities of these trials." Mr. Murphy talked about due process and equal protection. The previous cases -- granted there were lots of legal issues and procedural matters that needed to be dealt with. However, when you look at -- when you look at those kind of -- those cases, when you look at the indictments, when you look at the level of those individuals and then you look at the resources that were available and the time that was allotted versus today you have these megatrials, you have individuals who are at the highest level, and now even if you accept a lot of adjudicated facts and even though some of the procedural issues might have been dealt with, when you look and you do the comparison, one would say how is it that Blaskic gets a fair trial and Prlic or Petkovic or Praljak or Stojic or Coric does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or Pusic does not get one. Why is that Kordic can have so much time? Or Naser Oric, who is basically half of a count, has more time than we have? I don't want to get to trial -- the issue of whether one ethnicity gets more time than the other. I think that's not the case. What we're talking about is, if you go back in history when this institution was flush with money and they wasted it, in part they were having very long trials on minor individuals, granted they didn't have anybody else, but now we're at the stage where the international community is rather impatient. But they need to understand we're rapidly coming up to the 60th anniversary of Nuremberg. Nuremberg was the first step, was the very first step in establishing international criminal law as we know it today. That was the very first step. But what is Nuremberg really known for also? For a flawed process, an appeal process where they gave them 15 days essentially. A trial process where, well, where the Defence was heavily disadvantaged. I'm not even to go into the common purpose, the joint criminal enterprise, because I think that is flawed and is still flawed and unfortunately this Tribunal accepted that flawed concept. But when we look at Nuremberg, we see -- we see, yes, it was a positive step forward. However, it was somewhat of a victors' justice because it was rushed. The Defence were not given sufficient time to prepare. They were not given sufficient resources. I don't think we want to be in that position, and I think every Judge, every Judge has to stand on his or her own and say -- look in the mirror at the end of the day and say, "I gave them the very best trial I possibly could. Not because the Security Council's pressure that they're going to close down the institution and therefore I must rush them, but, realistically speaking, you know, I gave them the very best possible trial I could in light of the complexity of the trial." We all understand that the trials cannot take on for four or five years. We're trying to work as best as we can. But there comes a limit where if you try to make the procedures so short and try to have so many -- cut so many corners that effectively you're not providing a fair trial. And I must go back and ask all of us in this courtroom would any of us want to be tried in this fashion? Would we want to have a president of a country that we represent tried in this fashion? No. Would any member of the Security Council, would Mr. Bolton like to be an accused over here? I doubt it. Would President Bush like this process? Would Putin like to be here under this process? Granted the Russians are a little upset over the Milosevic death, but frankly speaking, we should be providing the sort of a trial that all of us wants for ourselves. And I -- I agree with the Prosecution that they're entitled to put on their case. They worked very hard. They do have a client as well. Their client are the victims. Their client is the international community, and I fully support their right to put on their case, because if they don't get to put on their case then somehow I'm going to be restricted as well, but they fulfil a particular function and that's why the Prosecution has to be independent in deciding who they're going to indict, how they're going to indict, what they're going to indict on. But the Defence at the same time has to be given the sufficient resources, the sufficient time to put on their case and to defend their clients in this system. And the system is adversarial. It's not Anglo-Saxon, it's adversarial. We are moving closer to the civil system and I don't have a problem with that. Mr. Murphy spoke about that. But it is adversarial, and, as Mr. Murphy indicated, the closer we go -- and I -- I must disagree with President Pocar when he says this is more of a Judge-control process now, as if we've gone -- we've stepped into the civil -- civil law land. If that were the case, then we're in deep trouble because effectively what is going on is, Judges are making the rules and circumventing the Statute and the Statute can only be amended by the Security Council. And what Mr. Murphy was pointing out and I had pointed this out in the past and let me -- let me repeat it: By effectively crossing that line, it means that we don't get the protections that an accused would get under the civil law system while at the same time by curtailing our rights to cross-examine, you are taking away the -- the necessary tools that we need. That's why cross-examination, the right of confrontation is so important in the adversarial position because of the different role the Prosecution plays. And that's why making a record is so important as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stewart, but please be brief because everything has already been said. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I thought everything had been said, I wouldn't say anything at all. But I will be brief. Your Honour, there is no dissent from Mr. Petkovic's Defence team from what Mr. Murphy said about the Prosecution case or anything else for that matter, nor am I going to enter into a debate this afternoon about the degree to which a fair trial can be waived. The simple position is, we would not contend that there's some general right to waive a fair trial. There are certain aspects that can be waived but that's for an another day. Our position in principle is simply this: That one cannot assess the time properly needed to prevent -- to present the six defence cases here until the Prosecution case has been presented, because it's the Prosecution case then that has to be answered. So that's the earliest point at which it can be properly assessed and it has to be kept under continuing review because the basic principle is that the Defence have to have throughout the trial sufficient opportunity and sufficient time adequately to present their defence, and the right to an expeditious trial is to be fitted within that basic right. The trial can go and should never go faster than is entirely consistent with that essential right. And that we -- I speak for Mr. Petkovic, with Ms. Alaburic this afternoon. I don't claim to speak for any other defendant, but so far as any other defendant supports that principle -- those principles and that approach, we would be delighted, because we say that's essential. What one cannot do is use the defendant's right to an expeditious trial against them to cut away at their essential right to have sufficient opportunity to present their own cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Murphy was getting on his feet, but perhaps if his colleagues have already addressed the issues he wanted to it address.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think they probably have. I just wanted to make sure that Judge Trechsel's question was fully answered, and I think it can be answered, Your Honour, really by -- by looking at -- I think it's Article 12 of the Statute that says that the Judges of the Tribunal have to be independent. Of course there will always be political issues regarding the funding of the Tribunal and all those things and I myself hesitate to address those things in detail in open session in the courtroom, but I think the important point is that it's the duty of the Judges to remain independent from that and to continue to give a fair trial and -- throughout the lifetime of this Tribunal. If it should be that the Tribunal's life is cut short, which I personally don't think it will be, but if it should be the case then, Your Honour, the poor people who should not suffer from that are the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, yes, your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One moment, and I want to preface what I'm saying now by saying I appreciate very much in all sincerity the very principled comments that have been made by the Defence this afternoon. At the same time, I would be -- I would be delinquent if I didn't observe that once again today the Prosecution has used the least amount of time as anyone in the courtroom and yet here we are, and it would be our time, it would be the Prosecution case that would be cut. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What you have said has been entered into the transcript. Perhaps we'll have a break soon because we were to have our break in 15 minutes' time, but it might be best to have a break before the witness comes into the courtroom. But first I'd like to read out an oral decision that concerns the admission into evidence of documents. It concerns documents relating to. Witness BU. Witness BU appeared only the 12th of October 2006 the Chamber decides to admit into evidence the following documents as shown by the Prosecution since they have a certain relevant and probative value and now I will read out the numbers of the documents slowly. P 09713 [Realtime transcript read in error, "P 0971"] under seal. There is an error in the transcript so I'll repeat that P 09713 under seal. And there is still an error. I'll start again. You'll make me say it in English. P 09713 under seal. That's fine now. Then P 01839, P 01955, P 01966, P 0196 -- 976. P 01976. P 08289 under seal, P 099 -- P 09696 under seal. I'll say that again, P 09696 under seal. P 08477 under seal. P 08613, P 08615. The Chamber notes that the Defence is not requesting that any documents be admitted into evidence in relation to this witness. It's now half past 3.00. We'll have a 20-minute break and we'll resume at 10 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm just concerned about the exhibits that relate to Mr. Agic. Perhaps this is not the appropriate time, but if we have a few minutes at the end. We've checked the information that we wanted to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you stand up, please. I'd first like to make sure you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, say that you can hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you tell me your first and last name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Safet Idrizovic, the 28th of March, 1949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm the chief of security in a powerplant in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before an international or national court with regard to the events that took place in your country in 1991, 1992, 1993, and 1994, or is this the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have already testified. Could you tell us where you testified, before which court, and which case was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this court. I testified in the Tuta and Stela case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness in the Tuta and Stela case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question which is important. Were you interviewed by investigators from your country? Have you been interviewed by investigators from your country? You have been interviewed by OTP investigators, but I'd like to know whether investigators or judges from your own country have interviewed with regard to events that took place in your country, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. Very well, then. Could you please read out the solemn declaration that the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to provide you with some information, sir. According to the Prosecution, you'll be spending three days in The Hague to testify. So that means today, Tuesday, and Wednesday. He will first have to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution, and the Prosecution will also show you some documents, documents that you have certainly seen already or that you saw when you met the Prosecution yesterday or this morning. Once the Prosecution has completed its examination-in-chief -- the Prosecution believes they'll take four and a half hours, at first sight this seems to be quite a lot of time. Perhaps the Prosecution will make efforts to reduce the amount of time they need. The Defence will have four and a half hours for their cross-examination. You mentioned General Petkovic on a number of occasions. As a result, General Petkovic's Defence will have an hour and 30 minutes, whereas the other Defence teams will have 45 minutes each. The four Judges sitting before you may also put questions to you if they believe it's necessary. As a rule, when the Judges put questions to a witness, these Judges follow on from questions put to you, or we put questions to you because we believe that your point of view might be interesting with regard to the indictment and the questions that we are putting to ourselves. The questions we ask ourselves are of two kinds. Firstly, we want to know who did what exactly, and once we have obtained answers to such questions, we try to establish the role each individual placed [as interpreted] within the chain of responsibility. So it's within such a framework that the Judges put questions to witnesses, and this allows the Judges to go to the crux of the matter immediately. If you run into difficulties in the hearing, inform us of the fact. If you fail to understand the meaning of a question, don't hesitate to ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. The Chamber is here to help you if you feel you have difficulties of any kind. Everyone one and a half hour we have a break for technical reasons and also to allow you to have a rest. Having testified for three days, you'll certainly feel quite tired. That's why it's necessary to have these breaks. Mr. Scott, I believe that you will be conducting the examination-in-chief, so I give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, I would like to move relatively quickly through some of your background, but some of it is important to various aspects of your testimony, so it will take a few moments. I understand, sir, that you served your period of military service in the JNA during the approximate period 1969 to 1971; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During that period of service did you also receive training for reserve officers which was intended to qualify you as a commanding officer within the reserve units which were known at that time as the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in 1971, on leaving active service, did you continue as a reserve officer in the Territorial Defence in the Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in addition to being -- acting in that capacity at the time you were also employed professionally as a schoolteacher in the elementary school -- in an elementary school in the municipality of Jablanica during that time period?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You then -- you began a course of study at the university of Zagreb, and you received a degree in political science; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You received a degree, I believe, in 1979.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Having obtained that degree, then did you go to work for the Ministry of Defence office in the municipality of Jablanica from approximately 1979 to 1983?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges briefly, please, when you served in that particular capacity what were you -- what was your job description, as it were? What were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my responsibilities was prescribed by the law on defence that was in force in the country at the time. My duties involved recruiting young men, sending them to serve in the then JNA, and then assigning them to reserve JNA units or to Territorial Defence units, and monitor the preparation for defence of the municipality, make defence plans, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said a moment ago you continued in this position -- acting in that capacity in addition to teaching school until approximately 1983. And then is it correct, sir, that you worked for a couple of years until approximately 1985 in essentially private business?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I understood you correctly. When I worked in the ministry, I was not working at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me. You did then -- yes. When you took up your position with the Ministry of Defence, that was then a full-time job; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My mistake. Forgive me. And then did you spend a couple of years, until 1985, in private industry?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't private. It was socially owned, and it was a catering establishment. It was not privately owned. It was not state owned. It was what we called socially owned, as all things were in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then, sir, in approximately 1985 did you return to what was considered active military service as commander of the Territorial Defence in Jablanica until approximately 1988?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that your rank at that time was captain first class?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, is it also correct, then, from about 1988 and really continuing until the present time you then took up responsibilities as chief of security at one or more hydroelectric facilities in the Jablanica area?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And I just said this but just to be clear, you continue in that position until the present time; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to 1990, can you tell the Judges based on your having lived in this area for a very long time what the approximately demographics of Jablanica municipality was as of 1990 in terms of the various national or ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: In the papers you have the exact statistical data, but roughly speaking, between 71 and 72 per cent were Muslims; about 17.8 per cent, if I'm not very much mistaken, were Croats; and approximately 4 per cent were Serbs. As to the rest, they were other, Yugoslavs, or other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, the usher has just placed before you a bundle of documents which we'll be using in the course of your examination. If I could ask you please to look -- if you can find, please, number 8556. It should also be available in e-court. There are tabbed numbers there, and they should be in numerical order, so I suspect 8556 is going to be toward the back or bottom of the bundle, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can assist. 8556. It may be in the second bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Idrizovic, this is a document from the -- part of the 1991 census results. And if you can find the place that lists -- gives the information for Jablanica municipality.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. This does not give percentages, but do you see that for Jablanica municipalities it indicates that there were approximately 7.806 Muslims and approximately 2.346 Croats? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And does that generally -- is that generally consistent with what you said a moment ago just in terms of your actual life experience and observation in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it does, and it's not difficult to calculate either. Yes, it does coincide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for the -- for the Court's assistance, then are there also -- is there also a figure for Jablanica town, if you will, not the municipality or opstina, but indicates the town is comprised of approximately 1.839 Muslims and approximately 617 Croats among others?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I won't take the time to go through all -- other individual entries, but you'll see on the document it also gives the particular breakdowns, for example, the villages of Doljani and Sovici in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, moving forward the Chamber has heard a substantial amount of evidence concerning the political developments in approximately 1990 and the elections that were held toward the end of that year so I won't ask you a lot of questions about that. But can you tell the Judges, please, during -- in 1990 and in the following several years, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And had you during this time -- you say you were not a member but let me just ask you. Were you active -- would you consider yourself active politically during that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't. I supported the SDP as a multi-ethnic party but without any active participation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as a result of the elections that were held in approximately November 1990, can you tell the Judges what the election results were in terms of on a political party basis? Which party received the majority votes, and which party received, for example, the second most votes?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, the elections were - how shall I say? - democratic, if you can speak of democracy at all down there, and the elections expressed the will of the people, but what they showed was a catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you. Did the SDA party win the biggest portion of the votes and the H -- the party known as the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina win the second most votes in the Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle it was the nationalist parties that won in the elections, and the party that presented itself or represented itself as the representative of its people won the SDA, as the Muslim party, Party of the Muslim People won the largest number of votes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: -- because there were most Muslims. The other one was the HDZ because the Croats were the second most numerous ethnic group. The SDS received a lesser number of votes because there were about 4 per cent of Serbs. At that time, there was a bloc of multi-ethnic parties, multinational parties like the SDP, the Liberals, and the Ante Markovic party. I forget what that was called. And they won some of the votes too. But all in all, the national parties were victorious, and they set up their power and authority which was to be fateful for Bosnia-Herzegovina later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, at that time based on the election results, who became the president of Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the SDA candidate was put forward, Hamdo Sefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall who took the position of vice-president?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it must have been some Croat from amongst the Croatian ranks. That would have been normal given the set-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Moving forward, then. Can you tell the Judges, please, and again the Judges have heard a fair amount of this evidence, but did there come a time in 1991 when the JNA essentially seized all the weapons and equipment that had traditionally belonged to or been part of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did that affect, then, the position -- your involvement during this time if you were, if you continued to have any reserve capacity, or did that involve -- excuse me. Did that affect your involvement and others' involvement in the Territorial Defence in the territory of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: That was already a time of the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia. The war had already begun in Slovenia. In 1991 things were brewing up in Croatia, and war ultimately broke out there. The Territorial Defence in Bosnia was disarmed and everything spelt of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward from that but in 1991, can you tell the Judges, was there any efforts by the various ethnic groups or political parties to divide up various factories or companies in the area of Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It began straight away in 1990, as soon as the power had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult for normal people to understand what was happening, but let's say they would decide that a company which had been -- well, all the companies were, as we call them, socially owned, or most of them, and where the director was a Muslim that was going to be a Muslim factory then. Where the director was a Croat or a Serb, those companies became Serb companies or Croatian companies, whatever. Something took place that no practice or theory could explain. There had been no precedent of that kind anywhere in the world. Of course this led to conflicting situations. The people knew that nothing good could come of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: But the power -- powers that be are the powers, and they dictate what they want. It was not just one such case. There were cases of that kind all over the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, what if anything happened in particular concerning the forestry business or the forest resources in the area of Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It shared the fate of everything else, went the same way. In an area where -- which was plentiful in forests, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges which of the national groups are ethnic groups seized -- took charge of the forest industry, if we can call it that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to do that, but I was waiting for the interpreters. Up until that period it was a Serb who was in charge, but he was displaced, replaced, and a Croat was sent in his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you have any information or knowledge as to the way that the forestry resources then began to be used once the -- once it became essentially a Croat or Bosnian Croat enterprise?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have no information about that. I couldn't have had any information about that. However, the forests began to follow a different route, a different course than had been the case up until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, may I intervene, because we're talking about a forestry industry, but we are jurists, the Judges. Now, was this industry based on private property, or did it belong to the municipality or an ethnic group or state? What kind of industry was it? Who did it belong to? Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The state. This was a state-owned enterprise. The forests, at least that's what it says on paper, still belong to the state, the property of the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this replacement of a Serb director by a Croat, who effected this replacement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the political parties which decided about matters of that kind. It was the political parties that had come into power and held the power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that means that the Croats had the political majority and were able to nominate and appoint who they wanted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They cooperated very well together when it came to privileges. They had no problem in deciding things like that together with the SDA. The important thing was to take as much state property as possible, or to take property away from a group. They had no problem in deciding amongst themselves what would belong to whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when they appointed this Croat director, was the SDA in agreement with this? Did they agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if a few moments ago on page 44, line 7, you said -- or excuse me, line 2, starting at line -- you stayed, "However, the forests efforts began to follow a different route, a different course that had been the case up until then." Can you tell us more what you mean?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was lack of control and forests were being felled down uncontrollably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, if I can ask you to look next to Exhibit 9400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. You said that there was a massive and uncontrollable felling of the forests. Who perpetrated this? Were they the managers of the forestry industry? Was it the workers themselves, workers within the industry? Who were they? Who decided upon these changes, and who decided to exploit the forests in a different way like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the person who was the director. He could do whatever he liked. Unfortunately, that's what the situation is like in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the present day. Nothing has changed in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was the Croatian director who decided to change, to modify the way in which forests were exploited, timber was exploited; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the same happened in other areas too. This was no exception. What I wanted to say when I said what I did was that on all sides there was a mass destruction of general socially owned property, and the property was used by those in whose hands it was, who disposed of it. This wasn't the only case and example. This kind of thing happened in other places too. And that's what's going on in Bosnia today as well, although there is an international police force there, the IPTF or whatever it's called down there. And although they exercise control, the political forces down there are doing the same kind of thing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, let me move forward. I just asked you to look a moment ago at Exhibit 9400, which should again be there in front of you, and I assume it would be in the second of the two bundles.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Or you can look -- if you have it on the screen, sir. Whatever is easiest for you. Sir, in the past several years did you take it on yourself to prepare a chronology of various events or developments related to Jablanica in the early to mid-1990s?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I am president of the veterans union at present in Jablanica municipality. Otherwise, I'm a member of the leadership of that organisation since its inception.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, what Exhibit 9400 is.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm speaking too slowly. If you want me to speed up, I can do that. I wanted to continue, actually, and say that among our other affairs and the work we do we decided on the basis of documents, wartime documentation that we had in our possession, to compile a chronology of the events as they occurred between 1992 and 1995. And in going about this business, I was given the task of dealing with the period from the 15th of April, 1992, to the 15th of April, 1993, to the beginning of the conflict with the HVO. It lasted five or six years, and it's still ongoing. And on the basis of the documents that were accessible to me, I carried out that assignment. And then when I had completed the assignment, and since I had already entered -- well, started these proceedings, at least where we are today, I felt that it was a good thing that from that chronology I should extract what relates to the activities of the HVO, to extract those portions up until the conflict of the 15th of April, 1993. So that's the chronology. I have all these documents in Jablanica. These are just excerpts from the document as it relates to the HVO. Nobody asked me to do this.
