I did this at my own initiative because I considered that it would be -- that it would facilitate an understanding of the situation if one were to look at the chronology of events and the time sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could intervene for one second here. We don't have the original chronology and this seems to be an excerpt, and we can see from the very first sentence here, says that this is a supplementary to the gentleman's statement. I'm wondering if he has the chronology with him because that would be important for us. Since this is just an excerpt of what he had, and it would be important for confrontation purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the document in B/C/S, I can see that this was done on the 26th of November, 2004. What we have, it's an extract of a more voluminous document and, if so, are there any dates that haven't been included in your chronology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a chronology of all the events, but everything that concerns the HVO has been extracted from it, everything that concerns HVO activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this document only includes issues that concern the HVO. For example, on 28th of November, 1991, in Grude, things start. The HZ HB is established, et cetera, et cetera. So all that has been noted concerns the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying to understand you, so please tell us again what you have included in this chronology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chronology includes all the events that took place in the territory of the municipality, all those events, and this includes the way in which the authorities functioned. It includes party activities, the army, the minister of the interior, and the HVO. We in fact tried to use the documents we had to establish a chronology in order to depict the way life went on at the time. That included how the economy functioned, wartime production, the military hospital, wartime hospital, education. So we tried to provide a picture of life in Jablanica during that period of time. But all this was done exclusively on the basis of documents. It wasn't on the basis of what people could remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "we," if I have understood you correctly, this was a collective effort made by veterans and the municipality. So it was not just you who worked on this matter. It was a collective efforts. Is that how I should understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to clarify this because the witness constantly uses the plural. So what is his contribution and what is the contribution of others? I think that he said he was only involved in a certain period when it comes to this chronology. If I have understood him correctly, from April 1992 to April 1993. I think that's the period that he mentioned that concerned him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many veterans were there? How many of there were you in this group? And as counsel has said, did you participate in the work of the entire group, or was your contribution limited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, others continued with the work. I was focused mainly on this period. We tried to work in groups, in teams. We tried to divide the work up according to our age, our fields of interest, et cetera. We worked in different ways. But in the end there were five or six of us who remained active in order to bring things to a conclusion. Unfortunately, we haven't published the entire chronology because we can't find anyone to finance us. Money is needed to publish this. Otherwise, over 90 per cent of this chronology has been prepared for publication. So I was only involved in this period up to the conflict. As far as the time period after the 15th of April, 1993, is concerned, well, others could say much more about that period than I can, and that's why I didn't want to get involved in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you worked up until the 15th of April, 1993. And when did you start working on this project? Did you start on the 28th of November, 1991? Did you personally start working then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. That's when everything started, in 1991 when they said HB [as interpreted] in Grude was established. And then on the 20th or 21st of January, 1992, when the Republika Srpska was established. This doesn't represent everything. This is not even a 10th of -- of what has actually been prepared, not even a 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would request that this particular document, one, not be introduced into evidence for a variety of evidence, and that we not proceed with taking evidence from this particular document for the following reasons: One, we don't have the names of the other members. That would be helpful. Two, we don't have the documents that were used for each and every one of these occasions that are listed in the chronology so at least we could test to see what sort of documents were used, whether documents were available but not used, documents that should have been used but were unavailable. Thirdly, we don't know whether the chronology is based on the gentleman's knowledge, personal knowledge of the events or whether these are merely something that he compiled as a result of reading documents, drawing some conclusions. And I don't think that this chronology has any real probative value. It would be much more useful for the gentleman, since he's here, to describe to us what he recalls since he was there on the ground. I think that's much more valuable than presenting this particular chronology, because it does affect the right of cross-examination since he doesn't know that -- he cannot, for instance, cite anything in any of these entries. And the way the chronology is put, Your Honour, is like an expert report, in a sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the problems that the Defence have discussed, and the Judges might have this in mind, too, concerns the methodology used to draw up this document. Perhaps you could pose a series of questions in order to respond to the objections raised by the Defence if you believe that this document has such importance that it's necessary to deal with it. That's yet again another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did not in fact -- excuse me. Sorry, counsel's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I really don't want to interrupt the proceedings, but in fact the witness didn't answer your question as to when the document was prepared. He started describing the first event mentioned in the chronology, but he said nothing about when they started on this, and obviously this took place many years after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you answer that question. When exactly was the document prepared? And then Mr. Scott will take the floor. Please go ahead, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People won't understand this or probably don't want to understand this. I said there are documents for each event in the chronology. There are documents for all the material that I have and that you have. The documents were the basis used. If they prepared themselves adequately, then they have documents for everything that has been written down here. I have provided the documents If they haven't read them, that's their problem. If they don't want to read them that's their problem again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a pity that our decision on time for objections hasn't been made effective yet. Otherwise, things would be somewhat different. Ms. Nozica, what did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I -- I didn't want to raise an objection. I wanted to assist the Bench and the Prosecution. In addition to the statement -- or in the statement we can see that the witness provided the Prosecution with 65 documents, and if we count the events chronology, there are twice as many events as there are documents. So the argument just presented by the witness isn't correct or can't be correct if the number of documents he provided to the Prosecution is direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for saying -- for interrupting again but the witness hasn't answered the question again. The question was quite clear. Could the Prosecutor please put the question to the witness or may I ask this question. You're quite clear, when you put your question to the witness I paraphrased it and now the witness is lecturing Defence counsel and telling them what they should know. He should quite simply answer the question and say when the document was drafted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I answered that question, but obviously you don't want to understand my answer. Work on this document was done for years. Immediately after the war, as of 1995 we started preparing the documents. I also said and this has been recorded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have understood that, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we want to know is the date on which you decided to start working on this. In the document we can see Grude, November, 1991. We would like to know whether this date corresponds to when you started focusing on the chronology or did you start working on the chronology prior to that date. That's what we would like to know. We don't want to know that you all started working in 1991. Have you understood the difference? When exactly did you say, "We're going to start working on this subject"? Was it November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must be quite frank and say I don't know. There's a decision rendered by the Presidency of the organisation that concerns this matter, but I wouldn't like to say anything off the top of my head. I can't even remember the year. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask, Your Honour -- with the Court's indulgence, may I ask a few questions, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. Really I believe we have to stop the discussion. The Chamber will decide about the acceptability of that document. We have heard the Defence. We have heard the witness. We have heard the accusation -- Prosecution, sorry. So it is my proposal to continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor, and try to answer our concerns by putting an appropriate series of questions to the witness, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, what I understand is that sometime after the war was over, and you said a moment ago in 1995 this veterans organisation decided to prepare a chronology of events in Jablanica municipality essentially during the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And your part of it, your assignment, was from approximately April 1992 until mid-April, 1993? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look, please, at the exhibit itself, if you look at the second page of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since there is no decision yet, I'd like to add a few words. Mr. Scott asked a question about the chronology in the municipality of Jablanica, but the witness said that the chronology concerned HVO activities. So I could use that chronology to say what I was doing or Mr. Karnavas. This is just a partial approach to what the HVO was doing. It doesn't concern the chronology of events in the municipality of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is way out of hand. I don't think that there's any -- this would be like making an objection that no -- no one book or no one document is exhaustive. It does not purport to be anything else. It would be like objecting and saying someone has written a book and they didn't bring every source item in the book to court. It would be like saying that not every piece of history is covered in a particular book. This is a publication which, in fairness to the witness he has answered a number of questions put to him. It was started by a veterans' organisation in approximately 1995. His particular part of it, the part that he was given responsibility for, was for the period from the 15th of April, 1992, approximately, until mid-April, 1993. Now, when one looks at what I was about to do was to ask the witness to look at the second page, at least of the English translation of the document, and you will see that but for the entry of the 28th of November, 1991, you will see that indeed the first entry is April, 1992. Likewise, if you turn to the last page of the document, and the witness can confirm this, but I think the document is very clear, the document -- the document ends on the 15th of April, 1993. Now, that's exactly what the witness has been telling us over this past 20 minutes or so. If I might just go back, sir, and just for the record and then we'll move on -- perhaps the use of the document might assist the witness, it might assist the Chamber. It is not the Bible of everything that happened in the conflict, but it is one organisation's attempt to make an order which the witness has explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But let me just ask you, sir, just so the record is clear: No one at the Office of the Prosecutor asked you to prepare this document or told you what to put in this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The veterans, they were former combatants, Croats, ABiH, HVO, or were they only members of the ABiH or the Territorial Defence of Jablanica? Could you tell us who these veterans in fact were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were armija members. HVO members have their own organisations with its own name, Hvidra. Unfortunately, they have not yet joined forces. They should do so, because if they remain separate entities, well, this means nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling us that the former HVO members also have their own organisation, and the name of the organisation is Hvidra, but they haven't yet compiled such a document, and, if I understood your document correctly, you seem to be saying that your two organisations should join forces, should become one organisation. Is that how I'm to take your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least that's precise. Mr. Scott, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, moving forward, then, can you tell the Judges after the 1990 elections and the election of the municipal officials which you mentioned now some minutes ago, did the municipal authorities continue to -- to act throughout most of 1992 as multi-ethnic or multi-party authorities in the sense that they were members of the SDA, they were members of the HDZ, they were members of the SDS, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, ostensibly, yes. [No interpretation]. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll check to see whether the interpretation is being received now. It's functioning. Can you hear the interpretation now, sir? Yes, it's functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, you said a moment ago yes, ostensibly that was the case. Can I ask you please to look at Exhibit 624 in the first bundle of documents that you should have, or on the screen if you like. And are these the minutes of a meeting, a session of the Jablanica Municipal Assembly on the 22nd of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that on the face of the document and listing those present it indicates the participants from a number of political parties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just as -- simply as one example, if you go to -- I'm not sure in -- probably in -- the same in the Bosnian version, but the second page do you see that the first agenda item was talking about a camp settlement for displaced persons? Agenda item 1.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, if you go several pages down in -- through the document, would you please go -- turn through the document until you find agenda item 2. Tell me when you have that, please.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the place on the screen. I can't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it would be best for you to have a look at the documents. It's very difficult to use the screen, and personally I only work with documents that I have in my hand. Have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have agenda item 2, sir, is that agenda item concerning the -- the security situation in Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever have occasion in any of your capacities to attend such meetings as this or to see the minutes of meetings such as this?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that if we looked at a collection of the minutes through 1992, they would look something similar to this in terms of the various participants of the various political parties being involved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention forward to February of 1992. Again, the Judges have heard a fair amount of evidence about this, but can you tell us what happened in connection with the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, focussing specifically on Jablanica municipality? What did you see and what do you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this -- prior to this event, representatives of the Serbian people in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina stated their position, and they wanted to cease taking part in the work of the Assembly, and they wanted to secede and to establish a Serbian republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And there was a decision for a referendum at which the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina would say whether they were in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina remaining part of Yugoslavia or whether they were in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina becoming an independent state. If my memory serves me correctly, the referendum was to be held on the 28th of February and the 1st of March, 1992. According to the media who reported on the 28th in the evening, in municipalities where the Croats were in the majority participation in the referendum was either minimum or non-existent. On the following day, the Croats who had participated in the referendum proclaimed independence, secession from Yugoslavia. And the next -- the next day they started immediately with the blockade of Sarajevo, and then things unfolded in the way that they unfolded. And on the 15th of April, a full-scale war had erupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. A couple of things there. When you say the 15th of April, you're now referring to 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I wonder if there was a mistake in the -- in the transcript, in the answer of the witness. Did he -- did you speak about the municipalities where Croats were in the majority or Serbs? Because then it is -- it is said at the end of your last answer that -- that on the following day the Croats who participated in the referendum proclaimed independence, secession from Yugoslavia, and the next day they started immediately with the blockade of Sarajevo. So I believe that you were speaking about the Serbs and not Croats, because in the transcript it is Croat which is being written. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, you just nodded your head in an affirmative way. Are you answering Judge Prandler's question that he is correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Say so aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why there was this confusion. I said that given what the Croats wanted, Bosnia-Herzegovina gained independence. And immediately on the following day - perhaps I wasn't clear - the Serbs blockaded Sarajevo and what happened, happened. That's what I wanted to say. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question that was put to the witness was what was going on in Jablanica. It might save a lot of time if the witness was not giving us a narrative about events in the whole of the former Yugoslavia but confined himself to the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I was thinking. You did political science studies, so -- you're not here as an expert in the social science sense, but you're a witness about the municipality in Jablanica. So please restrict your answers to Jablanica. Because if you incorporate the geopolitical and geostrategical considerations or whatever, then we're going to waste a lot of time, and what we're interested in is your experience of Jablanica. So please try to focus on that, exclusively what went on in that municipality. Mr. Scott, try and set that framework and ask your questions focussing on Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- I think I did, as Mr. Murphy said, but I will try to do better.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention specifically, because the Judges have heard about the referendum in general, and I want to ask you specifically questions about what happened where you lived, in Jablanica, during this time. And you said a moment ago on the first day -- to your knowledge on the first day of the referendum the Croats did not turn out to vote but on the second day they did. Now, that's where we are at the present time. Did you learn any information or come to know in Jablanica around that time what, if anything, had happened between the first day and the second day, leading to the Croats voting on the second day, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Jablanica is concerned, what I said a moment ago does not relate to that. In Jablanica, the necessary number of people voted the very first day. Of course, the voters we know don't vote according to ethnic group [as interpreted]. The media reported that in areas predominantly inhabited by Croats not enough people went to vote, that's what I said, on that first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I repeat my question to you, sir. Do you know what, if anything, happened between the first day and the second day that caused Croats to vote on the second day?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving then after the referendum to approximately April, 1992, was something called the War Presidency or Crisis Staff formed in Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us about that, please, briefly. How was that formed, and how was the War Presidency or Crisis Staff different than the municipal -- existing municipal government?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: The statutes or the constitution at that time in case of war the decisions are made by the narrow bodies, not the parliaments, the narrow bodies formed by political parties in power in order to be expeditious and expedient, and that's how the War Presidency was formed and Crisis Staff, and it functioned throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at that time, as of April, 1992, was the Crisis Staff formed on a multi-ethnic and multi-party basis?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It reflected that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Meaning, were there Croats, Muslims, and also Serbs on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I'm a bit lost here. You said during the war. Now, who was the enemy? Because if there were Croats, Muslims and Serbs, who then was the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was another enemy, one more. Well, the Serbs were the enemy at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the enemy were the Serbs, and in the Crisis Staff there were Serbs as well; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because they were there. They lived there and weren't acting against the state in any way. Not all the Serbs had left straight away. There were 4 per cent of Serbs where we lived. They weren't -- didn't represent a power of any kind. People were just living there, and they were represented in the authorities in that ratio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 4 per cent of Serbs in the municipality of Jablanica were represented in the Crisis Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They had the -- the SDS had a deputy in the Assembly and in the Presidency as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps it might assist, Mr. Idrizovic, did that -- if I ask you, this was the case -- I asked you, at the beginning of this time, in April, 1992, did that continue to be the case throughout the period of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing is the same. The situation deteriorated from one day to the next almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me follow up on the President's question. Did there come a time when the Serb members of the Municipal Assembly and/or the Crisis Staff that the Serb members stopped being involved or withdrew or were kicked out?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Not during the time we're discussing now. We're discussing it in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you said it didn't happen at this time it, and we're talking now about April, 1992, and you said it didn't happen at that time. I take it then your question -- your answer, excuse me, that it did happen at some time. Can you tell us when it happened?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs or the majority of the Serbs from which portion the deputies were left Jablanica in the autumn of 1993. Before that, might I just be allowed to say, the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had proclaimed the SDS a terrorist organisation, and then the mandate ceased to be, the term of office of those people, because they represented a terrorist organisation. I think that was sometime in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you've said that they left in the autumn of 1993, but I think just now you said something about 1992. Can you clarify that, please? Perhaps it was translated wrong or transcribed wrong.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed the Serbian Democratic Party a terrorist organisation, and with that the deputies' mandate came to an end, the SDS deputies' mandates came to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in relationship to -- between the Crisis Staff and the Municipal Assembly, did the Crisis Staff take the place of or displace the Municipal Assembly, or did the Municipal Assembly also continue to function during this time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff took decisions when the Assembly was not able to meet, to hold sessions. And when conditions were created, the Assembly was convened, an Assembly session was convened, and then the Assembly would verify or not verify the decisions passed by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In April 1992, was a new organisation called the Territorial Defence established?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How is this Territorial Defence different, if at all, from the Territorial Defence that had existed as part of the JNA structure?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, the decision was taken to abolish the staff as it had existed up until then, because it was a tag of the Yugoslav People's Army, if I can put it that way, and the staff of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And approximately when was that, sir, if you recall any particular date?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: The beginning of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is this the same organisation, then, a couple of months later or so in June -- approximately June, 1992, became the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, please, and again we're talking now about Jablanica municipality, was an HVO armed organisation or military organisation formed around this same time, April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's in the documents somewhere. There is that decision somewhere there about the establishment of the HVO in the municipalities which were supposed to make part of the Herceg-Bosna part. Thereabouts, perhaps earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Between the Territorial Defence and the HVO as they then existed or becoming established in April and May, 1992, which of the -- which of the two organisations were better organised and better equipped at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I think the HVO was better organised and equipped. I have no proof of that, but I assume it was better equipped because logistically it was better equipped than the army, the BH army, and it had somebody to lean upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say it had somebody to lean upon, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they could rely upon the Republic of Croatia which I assume helped them in their -- helped the members of the HVO in their equipment and training and things like that, because they had taken part in the Homeland War in Croatia before that. So it was normal for Croatia to help them in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During this time, sir, in Jablanica municipality did a number of Muslims join and participate in the HVO because it was perceived at that time to be the better organised and better equipped organisation?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: From Jablanica, as far as I know, there were just three soldiers in the HVO. That's not why Jablanica was characteristic -- or, rather, Jablanica was not characteristic of that like others were, like Capljina, Stolac, Mostar, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, did there come a time in April, 1992, that a bridge in the area of Jablanica called the Aleksin Han bridge was destroyed or partly destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of April, 1992. An attempt was made to destroy the bridge at Aleksin Han, which was -- or -- the sole route and connection between Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where was that bridge located in relationship to the town of Jablanica, north, east, west, south, what have you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: It is located 10 kilometres south of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in the direction of Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you and others know at the time who had destroyed or partly destroyed the bridge at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: An investigation into the event was conducted by the Ministry of the Interior. Some -- Ivan Rogic was seen in a truck and taken in for interrogation. The investigation, unfortunately, never reached completion because the person I named at that time and during the war, and today as well, is a very prominent member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was Mr. Rogic's position in the Jablanica area as of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was in various positions. From the elections onwards, he changed positions. He was in the party. Well, he was the number-one man in the HDZ of Jablanica, the main person as far as the Croatian people were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Around the time that the Aleksin Han bridge was partly destroyed, was another -- was there a tunnel called the Bradina tunnel either again destroyed or partly destroyed around that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where was this tunnel in relation to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: The tunnel was between Konjic and Sarajevo, on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Some 10 kilometres south-east of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: North-east of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry. What was the effect of the destruction or partial destruction of the bridge and the tunnel on transportation in or out of the Jablanica area at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: The bridge was completely damaged or one of the lanes on the bridge was completely destroyed. And UNPROFOR brought in a metal construction which bridged that damage, and then the bridge was in partial use after that, but heavy trucks couldn't cross over the bridge. And as to the tunnel, the roof of the tunnel caved in and the walls, and the road was partially destroyed too. But after it -- the debris had been cleared up it could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How soon after the bridge was partly destroyed did UNPROFOR build a replacement bridge?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Not long afterwards. It was a metal construction, as I've said, which spanned the area and enabled traffic in one direction, one lane. The work went on for some five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you this before -- I think it may be about time for the break, but if we can finish on this. You said a moment ago, however, if I understood you correctly, that even though this replacement bridge was build, it was not sufficient for heavy vehicle or truck traffic. Did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was there any alternative route, then, for truck traffic in that area at that time and, if so, what would be the alternative route?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the general assessment that these two explosions were supposed to make it impossible to communicate from Sarajevo with the Adriatic coast. Since this was in the Konjic-Jablanica area, the eastern border of Herceg-Bosna, they didn't need any roads linking Sarajevo to the sea. Instead of that, they built a series of roads, and the main road, which led from Jablanica across Posusje and Grude to Imotski and further on to Split. That was the main road. There were other roads that were built, too, because you had to link up all the territories of Herceg-Bosna, from Kiseljak to Split. And that project was almost completed. All that remained were two oases that hadn't been built, one around Fojnica and another around Prozor. And then you went on further across Prozor, Vran Planina, Tomislavgrad, once again to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps we can come back to that topic after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is now 5.25. We're going to take a 20-minute break and reconvene at about quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, could you clarify something for the Chamber, because as you know, the Prosecution's time is important for you. In the indictment, the indictment concerns Sovici and Doljani, and it relates to events that took place in April, 1993. We have spent about one hour discussing what took place in Jablanica municipality in 1992. So what are you trying to demonstrate? What is your objective? That's what I fail to understand. And not just me personally. The Bench as a whole fails to understand the objective you're pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for that. It is true that what is specifically charged in the indictment in terms of the crimes in Sovici and Doljani are quite specific to the period roughly April, 1993. However, as Judge Liu used to say on another case, Rome wasn't built in a day, number one, and there were a number of events leading up to those particular events. That's one part of the answer. The second part of the answer is notwithstanding that, it's part of the Prosecution case that there was a similar pattern of HVO takeovers in each of the municipalities, whether it was -- whether it was Mostar or Jablanica or Vares or Stolac, or what have you. And this is, as you know, Your Honour, we are now on a sequence of evidence in our case about the crime base in the various areas, and Mr. Idrizovic is the first witness, apart from any sort of introductory witnesses we may have had in the first phase, if you will, he is the first witness to talk about and to introduce Jablanica municipality. Therefore, he is providing a -- more of a historical lead-up to the core events. And it is relevant, because the case is built on a background of an increasing -- well, I don't want to say too much in front of the witness, frankly, Your Honour, but the case is, in theory, about the takeover of power in each of the municipalities, then leading up to the more core events, and that's what we're trying to do, albeit, I agree, slower than we would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the last answer we got to the witness which dealt with the bridge and the tunnel, if I understand the Prosecution correctly, if I'm reading the tea leaves, that is, or the coffee cup, as it were in the old country, I seem to be getting the impression that he is insinuating that the events in April, 1992, are part and parcel of the indictment. I fail to see how that is so. Is the Prosecution alleging now that the destruction of the bridge and the destruction of the tunnel, was that part of the joint criminal enterprise of the HVO? If that's so, then I'd like to know whether that is in the indictment. Is that something that I need to be aware of and to worry about? And also, is that what the witness is saying? Is there a linkage? Because as I understand it, at that time period in time the main aggressor are the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is in the indictment. I can go and point to the various -- not the charging -- not the -- not the destruction of the bridge per se, but what the indictment says, what the indictment says, if Mr. Karnavas would please give me a moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Take your time, take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Starting in the sections on -- starting with paragraph 18, those paragraphs give an overview of the history of the case, and among other things they talk about the series of takeovers of municipal power by the HVO in the various municipalities claimed, claimed, to comprise Herceg-Bosna, and that is indeed part of the Prosecution's case. Of all these events leading from 1991, and the Chamber well knows, that they've heard a substantial amount of evidence as to the formation of the HDZ, the formation of Herceg-Bosna in 1991, the dealings in Croatia, Mr. Manolic, all sorts of things. It is all one piece of events leading up to the conflict, the open conflict, in 1993. And Mr. -- this witness is the first witness to simply introduce these matters, background and history of these matters for Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the question of the tunnel and bridge is concerned, well, is that part of the strategy to take over power?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. We'll see. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I suspect also when it came to the forestry company, that's the same thing. But first of all, paragraph 18 is not mentioned in -- in the chart over here that this gentleman is going to be talking about paragraph 18, although that's fine. I'm not -- I don't want to go into any great details. But I fail to see how if it's not alleged in the indictment, because at this point in time it seems to me that what the Prosecution is arguing, that is of April, 1992, there is a joint criminal enterprise and this is part of that enterprise. This is -- keeping in mind that later on Mostar is going to be liberated, keeping in mind all of the events. Now, I think if I'm going to -- I need to have some precision, and in the indictment that is not alleged. These acts are not alleged. And to simply say in just one broad stroke that they were trying to take over the municipality, I can see if they're going into the structure, the political structure, the War Presidency decisions, but now we're talking about events in the middle of a war. Now, if they want to make some connection and ask the witness, you know, pose some more questions, I might be able to come around and say, okay, maybe this is part of their plan to establish a takeover. And while Rome wasn't built in -- you know, wasn't built in one day. I mean, we just seem to be starting someplace out in the stratosphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, can the questions you're putting to the witness you're trying to demonstrate how this takeover of power occurred in the municipality by the HVO. That's how we are to understand your series of questions. We'll see how things develop in light of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before the break you were talking about then the construction of a number of roads - excuse me - and before you continue on this can you tell the Judges around this time after the destruction of the bridge, around this time was certain heavy equipment appropriated or taken by certain parties from some of the large companies in the Jablanica area? And, if so, tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war in the territory of our municipalities, in the direction of Konjic, there was substantial work being carried out to reconstruct the road. Two big construction companies from Sarajevo were involved in this project. After Sarajevo had been placed under a blockade the equipment remained there on the road. Our wartime Presidency mobilised some of the heavy equipment and used it to construct the Jablanica-Posusje road, or some of it for that purpose, whereas another part of the equipment was used by members from the valley of Neretvica. They used it to construct a series of roads in the territory of the municipality of Konjic and further on in the direction of Fojnica. Several roads were built. I don't know how many exactly. I don't know whether it's really important for me to go into the details now. So some of the equipment was mobilised, and other material, other equipment was taken to Neretvica and used to construct roads for the HVO over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. On that point, sir, in the interests of time let me just ask you, did you observe at the time or come to know that this extensive road building that you observed happening in the Jablanica municipality and elsewhere, Konjic, was related to Herceg-Bosna consolidating communication and transmission lines in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. I can understand trying to assist the witness, but this goes beyond the pale, and I'm not really objecting normally as much as I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us sir, can you simply tell us what did you see happening in terms of the roads being built in relationship to various cities and lines of -- means of access to various parts of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's a decision from the War Presidency in our municipality according to which all men and equipment should be built on the Jablanica-Posusje road of salvation, the so-called road of salvation. You have this document. A number of other roads were built linking up the positions with inhabited places, et cetera. These roads are still in existence. I can provide you with a list if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at Exhibit 273 in your bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document doesn't have anything to do with the roads, though, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It has to do with the freedom of movement, Your Honour, which roads are often used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you see this document at the time or come to know of this document, about the ability to move around and through Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen the document before, but we all felt the consequences of this. The HVO was our embassy and our customs house. It was everything for us. If you wanted to travel somewhere, the HVO had to issue a certificate, as if I came to the Netherlands and I'd need a passport and a visa to come here. So we needed an HVO certificate. Naturally, I understand why Boban intervened. These certificates were being issued for money, and many people were in a position to print out these certificates and to sell them. So then Ivan Rogic was the only person authorised, and you could only leave the municipality with the relevant document bearing his signature. That's how things worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what is reflected in this document, that is the content of that document, is that what you saw and experienced, you and other inhabitants of Jablanica, during this period mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we all experienced this. We couldn't leave the municipality and set off in the direction of Croatia without having received authorisation from them. I personally went to Split on two occasions during that period of time. My father was in hospital over there, and I couldn't have gone there without a certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there any -- were you involved in any discussions or conversations around this time or with the municipal authorities in Jablanica as to why it was that either Mate Boban or Ivan Rogic or only the HVO could issue such certificates?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: No. How could one have discussed? It wasn't possible to go anywhere without a certificate. There was nothing to discuss in Jablanica, since someone up on Risovac wouldn't let you through. That was the end of the discussion up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any involvement -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I see this order issued by Mr. Mate Boban addressed to the Municipal HVO Staff in Jablanica. If an inhabitant of this place left the town without the certificate in question, what could happen to him? Does this mean that the town was under the control of the HVO forces and, as a result, you had no freedom of movement? You said -- you yourself said you wanted to go to Split on two occasions. You said you wanted to go to Split but weren't able to go there. What would have happened if you had left the city? It wouldn't have been possible for you to leave? What were the risks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't understand me correctly. I receive the certificate and I went to Split. I went to Split after I paid for the certificate. But you couldn't have left the town without a certificate because they'd stop you at the first HVO check-point. It's as if you arrived at the airport and you didn't have a passport, so they wouldn't let you through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the exit of the place there was a check-point then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not right next to the town but in territory under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if someone was controlled and had no certificate, what would happen to that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He'd have to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, moving to another topic, can you tell the Judges, during this time, we're now in approximately April, the spring of 1992, did it ever come to your attention that any military officers from the Republic of Croatia came into the Jablanica area?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in April or a little later, General Mate Sarlija arrived or Nijaz Batlak, as you wish, a Croatian general, a Muslim, and he had about 40 soldiers, it was a mixed formation and he said he was someone who would gather all the forces together and go and to raze the blockade of Croatia

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we come to Mr. Daidza, did you observe any other military coming into the Jablanica area before or apart from Mr. Daidza?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time people moved around freely. There were no problems. Later we found out that a member of the former JNA, Dzavid Balija, who was an Albanian by nationality but was married to someone from Jablanica, well, this member came to see us. At the time, everybody in Bosnia wanted to leave the JNA join the Territorial Defence, et cetera. The man came to us and we accepted him. And later in July and you can find this in the documents we in fact found out that the HVO security service had infiltrated this man amongst us. The aforementioned Daidza would be appointed to our command although he wasn't competent to this. And on the same day our commander was arrested, they sent this Daidza to be our commander. Naturally when they arrived we arrested him and kept him in prison for two days and expelled him from the municipality. He never returned. Unfortunately, I haven't got time. I could go into the details. But we had people who had been infiltrated amongst us throughout the war and they acted as disruptive forces amongst our ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know if any military advisors from the Republic of Croatia were involved with the Territorial Defence in the Jablanica area during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really understand the question. Military advisors, I don't really understand what you mean by that. There were various individuals who would come and offer assistance, but I don't really understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. That's my terminology. When you say various people came and offered their assistance, were some of these people from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about anyone coming from the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again staying on April, 1992, can you tell the Judges who became the head of the Territorial Defence in Jablanica municipality at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, the Defence Staff was established. Zijad Salihamidzic was appointed as the commander. Kopilas Stipo was appointed as the Chief of Staff, and I think there were 23 or 24 members of the staff. One of them was a Jew, one was a Serb, I think there were four or five Croats, and one was a Muslim. The HVO in Jablanica proposed men of its own and this proposal was accepted. There was Marko Zelenika who came for about a month.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreter didn't get the last part of your answer. You said Marko Zelenika came for about a month. And then what happened? Or what else did you say?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then he ceased performing those duties. He ceased coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And after Marko Zelenika ceased participating, was that the end of the participation of Croats in the Territorial Defence in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the officers are concerned, yes. As far as the soldiers are concerned, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you become a member of the Territorial Defence Staff on about the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the Territorial Defence attempt to have the HVO or Croats are the HVO, excuse me, participate in the Territorial Defence and come to meetings of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the documents that I provided the Prosecution with, you can see that on a number of occasions attempts were made to sit down, discuss the subject, but it was all to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please to look at Exhibit 321. Actually, my apology to everyone in the courtroom. Could I please ask you to look first at Exhibit 186. Can you tell us what that document is and what that was about?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the beginning of the war, May, 1992. Prior to this decision, there was a decree law, something like that, issued by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and which stated that the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina were composed of the Territorial Defence, the HVO, the Ministry of the Interior, and all other armed forces composed of individuals prepared to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was something to that effect. And after that document was issued, this decision was adopted according to which, given that there was the HVO, the Green Berets and the Territorial Defence in the territory of our municipality, they should be there in the municipality. Naturally at the time there was no discussion of open clashes or even of hidden clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look next at Exhibit 196. 196. And can you tell us what that is and how this document fit into the events at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was talking about a minute ago. It's the beginning of the war. They're suggesting that these individuals become members of the staff, Stipe Kopilas, Marko Zelenika, Ivo Zelenika, and Vjekoslav Skarda. Naturally apart from Marko none of them came to work there. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you to go to Exhibit 321, please. I asked you a few minutes ago before I by mistake skipped over a couple of exhibits, were there efforts by the Territorial Defence to continue to bring the HVO into involvement, cooperative involvement with the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the last attempt. After this attempt there were no others because they didn't respond. And afterwards, I think that there was a new decision issued on organising the staff since in the meantime because of the threats representatives or, rather, the Jewish representative and Serb had left the staff in Bos [phoen] and had left Bosnia. The Croats didn't want to participate, so all one could do at that point was to form the staff composed of members willing to participate in its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. There was a museum in Jablanica that contained artillery equipment from the second -- some artillery pieces from the Second World War; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges whether -- did there come a time in the spring or summer 1992 when some of those artillery pieces were refurbished to the point they could be used again, and then what happened to those artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were four howitzers. They were called Zis, Z-i-s They were the 100-millimetre howitzer. And all of them were refurbished, equipped to work. At the time we didn't have any active combat operations. We had passive positions towards the Serbs on Mount Prenj. We didn't need them, so we sent two to Sarajevo, to Igman, Mount Igman, one to Konjic, because they had constant contact with the Serb army in the vicinity of the town. And the third was given to Jasmin Jaganjac when he was preparing to deblock Mostar, the operation to lift the siege of Mostar. And let me just tell you that we put at the disposal of Jaganjac 80 of our fighters in liberating the northern portions of Sarajevo. They took part together with the HVO in the area of Jasinjabovic [phoen] and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, sir, two went to Sarajevo to Mount Igman, one went to Konjic, and one went to the Mostar HVO.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: One to the -- yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir this brings us to the appointment you started talking about a moment ago. Can you tell the Judges about this Daidza who came on the scene at that time and how he came involved?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: He came uninvited. He and his army, he and his soldiers started to behave brazenly. The first thing he did was to use the media to attack us in the Territorial Defence. Then he would walk around the villages with a car full of sweets, and he would hand the sweets over to the children and they thought he was Father Christmas, that kind of person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before, sir, before you continue on with that, do you know where Mr. Daidza came from or who had sent him into the Jablanica region? If you know.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: He was an immigrant. He was a criminal from World War II. Until changes occurred in Croatia, he didn't dare come to Yugoslavia. As far as we know, he was invited by somebody from Croatia and given the rank of general. I don't know what the regulations in that republic and who can hand out ranks of general left, right, and centre, but he came to us as a general of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you wish to intervene on that point? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I want to say that this man, upon his arrival in Croatia -- or, rather, before -- he was a United States citizen before he arrived in Croatia throughout that time, and if he was a citizen of the USA with a passport, then the witness cannot be allowed to proclaim the man a criminal without any proof and evidence. This is completely unacceptable and an insult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, it is also not acceptable and according to the rules that you stand up and testify. You have -- far from asking a question, you have stood up like a witness to make a statement that differs from that of this witness. If you do not agree with what he is saying, certainly your lawyers will take advantage of that, but I think you should also respect the rules, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I will respect the rules and procedure, but to call someone a criminal and nobody to get up to object, well, I really don't know. And I do apologise. And in passing, we're going to show who sent him and whose general he was in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in speaking about that general, you said that it was a criminal from World War II. General Praljak has told us that he was an American citizen and that he held a USA passport. So what allows you to say that he was a World War II criminal? Where do you get that from? Because it's very serious to accuse somebody of things like that without proof and evidence. So what has prompted you to say that? What allows you to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were told that by his neighbours and relatives, because he is a native of Blagaj, Mostar, that's where he originated from and when he came to Bosnia-Herzegovina territory they told us where he was from. We had never heard of him before then or seen him. So what I said now, just now is how we saw him, and his neighbours and his relatives told us that. Now, if I have violated any procedural rights, I apologise. Perhaps I used a strong word, but that's how we saw him. That's how we experienced him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that it was the family -- his family members or neighbours that said that. But you are an educated man. You went to university, the university of Zagreb. You're a specialist in political sciences, and you have some knowledge. You know that if you are a citizen of the United States and if you come from a country other than the United States there's a whole procedure that the authorities engage in, the American authorities, to see whether you are a delinquent, whether you are a wanted person, or whatever. The United States authorities look into all that when somebody comes in from another country. So you are stating facts -- you are stating some sort of fact that an intellectual of your level and standing should not do without having proof and evidence, or did you not know that you can only become a citizen of the United States of America after you go through a whole system of checks and proofs and verifications? Do you know that or not? If you don't know that that is the case, then say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know that, and I doubt that he was in fact a citizen of the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Praljak tells us that he is a US citizen, he must have proof of that, but we'll go into that later on in due course. Mr. Scott, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you began to tell us, I think, a few minutes ago when you first mentioned this Daidza's involvement, did there come a time when the commander of the Territorial Defence in Jablanica was arrested by Mr. Daidza or people acting on his orders?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: At a certain point he stormed the hotel in Jablanica, stormed into the hotel where the commander of our staff was with 15 or 20 well-armed soldiers. He arrested the man, took him away to the Herceg Stjepan Brigade headquarters at Kostajnica, near Konjic, and then he issued an orders to appoint Balija Dzavid as commander and serve in his place, and by doing so he put himself in the role of the Supreme Command who can appoint or relieve of duty Staff Commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we go further into that, can you give us any approximate date when this occurred or even the month or year?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Between the 10th and 12th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge did Mr. -- I shouldn't say Mr. Daidza. Daidza was a nickname; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think you've said it before, but do you know the correct name of this man?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: He has two, one Croatian and one Bosniak. Mate Sarlija or Nijaz Batlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when Daidza arrested the head of the Territorial Defence on who was that at that time for the record?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Salihamidzic

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When Daidza arrested the commander was there any explanation given as to his authorisation or power to take such an action?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. He was the commander of some brigade and he issued orders to replace this man and to appoint the other man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that he was taken -- the commander was taken to the Herceg Stjepan Brigade near Konjic. Of which military organisation was the Herceg Stjepan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that Daidza then attempted to put another commander in the place of this other gentleman. What was the name of that man?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Dzavid Balija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened with him?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when he came to us to be our commander, we arrested him. And two days later expelled him from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did you arrest him?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Because he was a Trojan horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the commander from one army replaces the commander in another army and then appoints a new one. I don't know if there's a better expression than that. We in Bosnia say that it's one of those eggs that the bird places in somebody else's nest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward to -- or in the summer of 1992, who were the principal leaders or figures, full in the HDZ in Jablanica at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: There were three men mostly who assumed all these posts in the they were Matan Zaric, Ivan Rogic, and Mirko Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give us the second name? You mentioned Matan Zaric which is in the transcript. Can you give us the second name, please.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Ivan Rogic. Ivan Rogic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Further in the summer of 1992, was there another attack on this same Aleksin Han bridge that you mentioned earlier today?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 8th of August, 1992. Some HVO units came to the bridge again, killed two of our men who were providing security on the bridge. They captured seven and took them off to Split. Two days later, they were returned to Grude, and from there they were taken over by our president of the municipality and chief of MUP. And in addition to other things, there is an HVO police report in Jablanica among your documents, among the documents you have Our engineers unit, after the incident on the bridge, found about 150 kilograms of explosives with all the necessary equipment to blow up the bridge. That was the second attempt to blow up the bridge, to destroy the bridge, which luckily was aborted for some technical reason. I don't remember exactly what it was. You might have it in your documents, whether because of humidity or whether the gunpowder was damp or whatever. Let me also say that those were the first victims that fell, our first fatalities during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please to look at Exhibit 388. A report from the HVO military police covering the period from the 6th of August to the 13th of August, 1992. Can I ask you please to turn to -- that is section called incidents. If you can find the section called incidents and on the English --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that a description, sir, if you look at that, is that a description at least in part of what happened at the Aleksin Han bridge at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to talk with these -- any of the ABiH members or soldiers who had been taken to Split? Oh, sorry. You probably didn't hear my --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us -- can you tell the Judges what they said had happened to them and why -- what happened in Split?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: They were interrogated but not abused, not mistreated. After the interrogation, they were sent back to Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward to September of 1992, can you tell us whether there was an attack on a check-point near one of the exit locations from Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was an attack at the check-point to the exit from Jablanica at the village of Jelacic, without any human casualties, luckily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know who carried out this attack?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't suppose -- you don't suppose the armija, BH armija attacked itself, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me persist in my question to you, sir. Do you know or do you have information as to who attacked that check-point?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going forward to October of 1992, did you ever learn about a meeting that was called by someone, and I'll ask you who in a moment, but there was a meeting called to discuss the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: The international community. Negotiations were conducted with respect to the Vance-Owen Plan or something like that. I can't remember exactly now what it was all about, but the plan never was accepted, and it implied the cantonisation of Bosnia, as far as I remember, on ethnic principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that context, sir, let me go back to my question then. In the context you just gave us, was there a meeting in Tomislavgrad to discuss the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: During the summer of 1992 there were attempts on our part of meeting. I think our representatives went to Posusje and Tomislavgrad for negotiations. And what you're asking me about now, the discussion on the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Tomislavgrad, well, I can't really answer that. I don't know whether that was the actual topic of discussion, the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a subject that was discussed elsewhere, not even in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. It was a subject discussed elsewhere. But I'm not clear I understand your question in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this, sir, and if it doesn't assist I'll move on. Did you ever or did one of your colleagues ever attend a meeting with a man called Zeljko Glasnovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't, but some of my colleagues did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Such as, in terms of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle it would always be the chief of MUP who went and somebody to represent the staff, either the Chief of Staff or the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was the head of MUP -- of the MUP at least of Bosnia-Herzegovina as of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: In Jablanica you mean. Emin Zebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zebic go to this meeting with Mr. Glasnovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, someone went. I can't remember who it was. I haven't got a note so that I can look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: There was some kind of meeting, and it's all in the document somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- then let's move forward then if you don't remember that. Did there come a time when the Croat members -- some of the Croat members of the MUP, we were just talking about the MUP, left the MUP to go to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That was already the autumn of 1992. And otherwise attempts were made to include the MUP of Jablanica and Konjic into the MUP of Bosnia. There were a number of attempts along those lines and finally members of the Croatian people in MUP in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina gradually left MUP and joined up with the military or civilian police. I don't know if they had a civilian police, but anyway, the HVO. People were given a salary there, and they were able to have a more or less normal status, whereas with us they didn't. That could have been one of the reasons, and the other was the efforts made or, rather, it was an attempt to establish HVO power and authority gradually in the police, the army, later on the demand to take over power fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 832. This is a report from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Ministry of Interior dated the 30th of November, 1992. Can I ask you, please, to look at the first couple of paragraphs of that report, and if you can tell that -- tell the Judges whether that relates to what you were just telling us about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that what was happening in the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Jablanica municipality around this time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. And this was a time when they insisted on MUP Herceg-Bosna or, rather, they began to exist parallelly, the two MUPs, and then a conflict of interests arose, if I can put it that way.
